task: For this synthetic writing exercise, use the fictional reporting notes to write a newspaper explainer for general readers. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 20, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: The Federal Airspace Safety Commission issued Airspace Corridor Rule 14-CR-2025 in March 2025, creating designated altitude corridors for commercial drone deliveries in large U.S. cities.
The rule takes effect September 1, 2025, and is the first permanent framework permitting commercial drones to fly beyond an operator's line of sight in urban airspace.
Under the rule, commercial drones may fly between 200 and 400 feet above ground level within designated corridors.
The rule initially covers 12 cities with populations exceeding 1 million; additional cities may apply for corridor designation beginning January 2026.
Drone operators must hold a Remote Operator Certificate and a corridor-specific operating permit, which costs $500 per year per operator.
The maximum payload for a drone operating under the rule is five pounds.
Commercial operations are restricted to the hours of 6 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time.
Drones may not operate within one mile of hospitals, schools, prisons, or emergency response facilities, regardless of corridor boundaries.
Commission Chair Janet Ortega said: "These corridors create a predictable, safe operating environment that protects both the public and emerging commercial operators."
The rule allows operators to use cameras and sensors necessary for navigation but does not require them to delete footage captured during deliveries.

Alan Thorpe, research director at the fictional Digital Rights Watch advocacy organization, said: "A drone at 300 feet with a package is also a drone with a camera, and the rule says almost nothing about what operators can record."
Three commercial operators — fictional companies Skyward Logistics, QuickDeliver, and AirRoute — have filed applications for corridor operating permits.
The Commercial Drone Alliance said the rule would "unlock hundreds of millions of dollars in investment in same-day delivery infrastructure."
Outside limited temporary waivers, the prior framework required visual line of sight. The new rule provides a permanent route to beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations within designated corridors.
The Commission estimates corridor drone deliveries could reduce short-haul delivery truck trips in covered cities by between 5 and 12 percent if widely adopted.
The rule does not address noise standards; the Commission said noise limits would be addressed in a separate rulemaking expected in 2026.
Corridor boundaries are determined by the Commission in consultation with local aviation authorities; municipalities have 30 days to object before a designation becomes final.
The Commission processed 3,400 public comments during the rulemaking period; the majority came from residents in cities included in the initial 12.
Commercial drone delivery has operated on a limited experimental basis in fewer than a dozen U.S. locations under temporary waivers; the new rule creates a permanent legal framework.
The five-pound limit excludes any payload above that weight, including larger grocery orders and many appliances. It does not categorically exclude a grocery order weighing five pounds or less.
Local air traffic controllers' unions raised concerns that the rule does not address how corridor drone traffic will be monitored and separated from low-altitude manned aircraft.
The rule's enforcement mechanism for operators who fly outside designated corridors or outside permitted hours is a civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation, according to the commission.
